correctness.rationale: For any zero profile, an effective defender covers all zeros outside its part. Any feasible function can be reduced without greater weight to one zero-free defender or two distinct effective defenders: two cover every zero because a zero belongs to at most one of their parts. With one defender, converting all positive vertices outside its part to zeros never raises weight and gives a_i+ceil((N-a_i)/p). With two defenders, converting every other positive within their parts to zero costs at most the unit saved, yielding F(t)=2+t+ceil((N-a_i-1-t)/p)+ceil((N-a_j-1-t)/p). Write t=qp+s: F(t)=F(s)+q(p-2); for 2<=s

originality.rationale: The 2024 defining source proves complete bipartite values and general bounds, but not the exact generalized p-strong r>=3 multipartite formula. Closest published r>=3 complete-multipartite record is ordinary strong Roman (p=2); the related total strong Roman result imposes an extra support constraint at p=2. The different k-strong Roman model is not equivalent. The correction produces a strict one-unit improvement and arbitrarily large gain over the old single-defender bound. Exact novelty remains contingent on indexed/unindexed literature coverage.
residual_risks: Semantic indexing is not complete; an unindexed equivalent p-strong r>=3 multipartite formula could exist.
The related k-strong Roman attack-pattern literature uses a different definition; no implication is asserted without a separate bridge theorem.
First public date is established from university repository metadata, but earlier unrecorded releases cannot be excluded.

value.rationale: The original p-strong Roman study identifies exact values for further graph families as a natural problem. This theorem resolves arbitrary part-size vectors with >=3 parts for every nontrivial p, using O(r^2) arithmetic, and exposes an unanticipated third-part congruence helper. K_(5,5,5) at p=4 genuinely needs weight 7 instead of the standard one-defender upper bound 8; fixed-p balanced tripartite graphs improve that bound by a quantity linear in part size. The result is a complete natural-family optimization, not a routine special-case substitution.
